title: The Ebony Kingdom
summary: Vampire Africa, a patchwork of kingdoms ruled by the Guruhi.

claims.text: All the vampire kingdoms of Africa together make up the Ebony Kingdom.
It now holds 11 lesser kingdoms, each under a Guruhi lord, split into smaller domains governed by magaji.
Laibon society is local and fragmented: a thin shared vampire culture spans the continent, but no single authority rules all domains.
Politics turn on the clash between tradition, backed by the Guruhi and elders, and the more progressive young Laibon.

title: Laibon Terms
summary: Common words of African vampire society.

claims.text: Laibon means an African vampire; in Maasai the word means shaman or medicine man.
In the Ebony Kingdom clans are called legacies, a word with a stronger family sense than clan.
A magaji is the leading vampire of a domain, much like a prince, from a Boko word for king.
Feuding within a legacy is thought unbecoming, though rivalries still happen.

title: Magaji and Rival Claimants
summary: How domains are ruled in practice.

claims.text: Only a lord can grant the title of magaji, but countless pretenders claim it, and in big cities a claimant may rule without the Guruhi patron knowing.
Guruhi kings are often old or distracted and may not care who is magaji if the kingdom is calm, so a domain can have two claimants or none and be truly lawless.

title: Akunanse
summary: The wandering storyteller legacy, called Weavers.

claims.text: The Akunanse take their name from the wise spider of Ashanti legend and are nicknamed Weavers.
They roam the continent seeking knowledge, take on beastly traits of spider, lion, hyena or snake with age, and are valued as advisors.
They are probably rooted in Ghana but no longer call any region home, and they care less about the Jyhad than any other legacy.
Legend tells of an Akunanse traveller named Hasani who crossed every kind of land in the 16th century.

title: Setites of the Ebony Kingdom
summary: Sub-Saharan Followers of Set, called Vipers.

claims.text: Nicknamed Vipers, they draw others under their sway while staying apart from Laibon politics.
They await the finding of the Grand Temple, which some think lies in the Ebony Kingdom together with Set, who withdrew there in AD 33.
Zhenga, a Setite, rules the criminal underworld of Mombasa and wants to claim the city outright.
The Guruhi are nicknamed Kings and hold the kingdoms of the Ebony Kingdom.
Their looks shift with their moods, by turns hideous and angelic; their legend says a god cursed the founder to be only as fair as the founder's soul.
Their legacy Disciplines are Animalism, Potence and Presence.

title: Ishtarri
summary: Outsider spies and diplomats, called Gluttons.

claims.text: The Ishtarri claim the name of the Babylonian goddess Ishtar and are nicknamed Gluttons.
They are not native to Africa, never hide it, and have made themselves vital to Laibon society through diplomacy and spying without trying to unseat the Guruhi.

title: Kinyonyi
summary: The travelling legacy that fetches and carries, called Nomads.

claims.text: Their name comes from the Luganda word for bird, and they travel more than any other legacy.
Other Laibon turn to them to obtain goods or carry out tasks, for a price.
They began as outsiders and keep their own organization apart from mainstream society.

title: Naglopers
summary: A debased and cruel legacy, called Horrors.

claims.text: Naglopers are a cruel, debased legacy nicknamed Horrors.
Few are social, and the socially gifted ones count among the most frightening psychopaths.

title: Osebo
summary: The hot-blooded warrior legacy, called the Pride.

claims.text: Named for the proud leopard of Ashanti legend, the Osebo are among the most numerous legacies and are called the Pride.
They Embrace on impulse, all share a fiery temper, and often serve as warriors.

title: Shango
summary: Warriors and sorcerers devoted to the Yoruba god of storms, called Judges.

claims.text: The Shango worship the Yoruba god of storms, magic and war and have long been the power behind many magaji.
They uphold the established order, which often makes them allies of the Guruhi, and they keep quiet about their magic.
Laibon tales credit many fables to an old Shango named Jafari, who may never have existed.

title: Mla Watu
summary: A feared legacy that controls the dead, called Ghost-Eaters.

claims.text: The Mla Watu seek to command the dead rather than seek their counsel, which many Laibon find repulsive.
They want to be left alone, and most Laibon oblige them; the few who hunted them have tended to disappear.

title: Nkulu Zao
summary: The hunted childer of Zao-lat, called Soulsuckers.

claims.text: Their founder Zao-lat was found asleep by power-seeking magi and supposedly destroyed, drained by the strongest of them, who then hunted the childer.
Nobody knows how many survive, and some think the belief that only a handful exist is spread by the Nkulu Zao themselves.

title: Foreign Clans in Africa
summary: Western clans that live in the Ebony Kingdom.

claims.text: Malkavians and Ventrue in Africa resemble their clanmates elsewhere but have usually left something behind to seek refuge there.
Laibon call the Malkavians Hyenas and the Ventrue Blue Bloods.
Ghosts and hunters in the Ebony Kingdom are much like those elsewhere.
Instead of only Lupines, Africa has many kinds of beast-men, and the lines between kinds of supernatural blur more there.
